opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back.

I think it helps to separate two questions: whether scaling *works*, and whether it's *efficient*. People often treat those as the same thing, and they're not.

On the first, the scaling laws have been remarkably reliable. Add more compute, data and parameters and the loss goes down in a smooth, predictable way. That predictability is a big part of why so much money has flowed into the field.

But look at the shape of those curves. The improvements are roughly logarithmic in compute. To get each further step of improvement, you need to multiply your resources by some large factor, like ten or a hundred. So scaling is a paradox. In one sense it's an amazing success: we've found a recipe that reliably turns resources into capability. In another sense it's incredibly inefficient. Each increment costs vastly more than the last, and if you showed those numbers to a scientist in almost any other field, they'd say you'd hit steeply diminishing returns.

For a while that didn't matter much, because we started from such a small base. Going from a few thousand dollars of training compute to a few million, and then to hundreds of millions, was feasible. But you can't keep multiplying by ten. Training runs are already in the billions of dollars. A few more orders of magnitude and you're talking about a meaningful fraction of world GDP, plus physical constraints on chips, power and data centres. So pre-training scale-ups, as a driver of progress, have a natural horizon. It isn't a wall, more a slope that keeps getting steeper.

That's partly why the labs have shifted toward other kinds of scaling: reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks, and especially inference-time compute, where the model thinks longer before answering. Those have produced real gains. But they change the economics in ways people haven't fully absorbed. With pre-training you pay once and amortise the cost over every user. With inference scaling you pay every time the model is used. If much of the capability gain comes from letting the model think a hundred times longer, every query costs about a hundred times more. That's a very different picture from "we trained a smarter model and now everyone has it cheaply." The returns there also look logarithmic, so you hit the same diminishing-returns dynamic, now as a recurring cost rather than a one-off.

So my overall view is this. Scaling alone, in the brute-force sense, probably isn't a cheap or fast route to extremely powerful AI. It may still get there, because enormous resources are being devoted to it and because these systems might start to speed up AI research itself. That feedback loop is the main thing that could break the diminishing-returns picture. But absent that, I'd expect progress to depend more and more on algorithmic ideas and efficiency gains, not just bigger numbers.

From a safety and governance point of view, I think that matters. If capability depends heavily on enormous, visible, expensive compute, both in training and at deployment, that gives us natural chokepoints and some warning time. If the frontier shifts toward algorithmic breakthroughs, that picture becomes much less comfortable. So understanding the limits of scaling isn't just an academic forecasting question. It shapes which levers we'll have when it counts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the big thing people miss is that scaling was never going to go on forever in the form it took from roughly 2019 to 2024. The scaling laws themselves are actually fairly pessimistic if you read them carefully. They say that to get a constant improvement in loss, you need to multiply your compute by some large factor. So each step of progress costs exponentially more than the last. That's a deeply unfavourable relationship, and the only reason it felt like rapid progress is that the industry was willing to increase spending by orders of magnitude in a very short time.

And that's the crux. Those orders of magnitude came from several sources at once: hardware getting cheaper, algorithms getting more efficient, and above all the amount of money being poured in. The money part is the one that can't continue indefinitely. You can go from a few million dollars for a training run to a few hundred million, to a few billion, maybe to tens of billions. But you can't keep multiplying by ten every couple of years for long before you hit the scale of national budgets or the whole economy. So the pre-training scaling era had a built-in expiry date, and I think we've already seen the industry quietly acknowledge that by shifting emphasis to things like reinforcement learning on reasoning and inference-time compute.

Now, those new axes are real, and they've bought a lot of capability. But I'd make a similar point about them. The gains from letting a model think for longer at inference time are impressive, but they also appear to be logarithmic in the amount of compute. Ten times more thinking buys you a fixed increment rather than a tenfold improvement. And inference compute is paid every single time you use the system, not once at training, so the economics are if anything harsher.

So where does that leave us? I don't think it means powerful AI isn't coming. It means the shape of the trajectory matters. If progress depends on resource growth that must slow down, then we may be heading into a period where capabilities keep improving but more gradually, driven by algorithmic ideas rather than brute force. That's actually quite important for people thinking about risk, because a lot of the fastest-timeline scenarios implicitly assumed scaling would just keep delivering. If it doesn't, we may have somewhat more time than the most aggressive forecasts suggest, though I'd be cautious about leaning on that too heavily. New ideas can arrive at any point, and historically the field has found a new lever just as the old one started to run out.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish two questions. One is whether scaling up the methods we have now could get us to extremely powerful AI. The other is whether that’s the route we will actually take. Even if scaling alone would eventually work, improvements in algorithms could turn out to be a much faster way of getting there.

The successes of scaling are striking, but they don’t establish how far it will go. You can have a trend that holds over many orders of magnitude and still encounter a limit. And there’s a further question about what exactly is improving: getting better at predicting text is measurable, but how that translates into the ability to carry out a long, difficult project in the world is less straightforward.

At the same time, I’d be wary of confidently declaring that there must be some barrier that scaling can’t cross. We don’t understand intelligence well enough to know that. A capability that looks as though it requires a fundamentally new idea might emerge from a system trained at a larger scale—or it might require a new idea that turns out to be quite simple.

So I wouldn’t want our thinking about AI risk to depend on scaling either definitely succeeding or definitely failing. A limit to this particular route wouldn’t establish a limit to artificial intelligence. It would change our expectations about the timing, and perhaps give us more time to prepare. But it wouldn’t, by itself, settle the larger question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish two questions. One is whether scaling up the systems we have will keep producing substantial improvements. The other is whether that process alone gets us all the way to extremely powerful AI. You could be quite optimistic about the first and still uncertain about the second.

We’ve seen impressive gains from increasing the amount of computation and data used in training. That’s a good reason to take scaling seriously. But it doesn’t establish that every important capability will emerge if you just keep going. There might be bottlenecks involving things like planning, learning from experience, or reliably carrying out a task over a long period.

And there are practical limits as well. You might run out of readily available high-quality data, or the cost of another substantial increase in computation might become prohibitive. Though those aren’t necessarily hard limits: people can find more efficient methods, or ways for systems to learn through interaction.

So I’m wary of confidence in either direction. ‘Scaling has worked so far, therefore it will get us all the way’ seems too strong. But ‘scaling must hit a wall before anything transformative happens’ also seems too strong. For thinking about existential risk, the important point is that uncertainty about the route isn’t a reason to dismiss the destination. We should take seriously the possibility that scaling, together with further algorithmic improvements, could get us there.
